title: Faculty meeting: departmental policy on student use of generative AI

lines.text: Let's get going. Item one is the generative AI policy, which the Dean wants by November. For what it's worth, I've chaired this department for eight years and I've never seen a policy question split us this badly.

Oh brilliant, another committee to draft another policy that students will ignore. With respect, we already have an academic integrity code. AI-written essays are plagiarism under the existing wording; we don't need a new document.

Quick data point. In our spring survey, 71% of undergraduates said they'd used ChatGPT on coursework at least once, and only 18% thought they'd broken a rule. From where I sit at the Centre for Teaching and Learning, the existing code is simply not being read that way.

I'd just gently add that detection tools are not the answer. OpenAI itself withdrew its AI text classifier in 2023 because of low accuracy, and the false-positive studies show non-native English writers get flagged far more often.

Speaking as a writer, my worry is different. When my novel The Salt Archive came out in translation last year, I found pirated copies of it in a training dataset scrape. Students should understand that these tools are built on other people's unpaid work.
Ingrid's The Salt Archive is exactly why I'm against blanket permission. With respect, if we let students run prompts on everything, we're teaching them that authorship is optional.

For what it's worth, the legal side is moving. The EU AI Act classifies AI systems used to evaluate students or determine admissions as high-risk, so any grading tool we adopt will carry compliance obligations from 2026.
And GDPR applies to anything students paste in. If a student uploads a classmate's peer review into a chatbot, that's personal data leaving the university. That's the part people forget.

I'd just gently propose a three-tier model per assignment: AI prohibited, AI permitted with disclosure, AI required. Each syllabus marks every assignment with one tier, and students attach a short disclosure statement when they use it.
Splendid, so now every essay comes with a confession form. Wonderful. Because nothing says rigorous scholarship like a checkbox. With respect, students will tick 'no AI' and move on.

Marcus, the checkbox isn't the point; the conversation is. Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language' argues that sloppy language enables sloppy thinking. That's the lesson: if a student can't defend a sentence in a viva, they didn't write it.

That suggests oral defence as the safeguard rather than detection. For what it's worth, the Russell Group published principles on generative AI in 2023 that lean the same way: teach AI literacy, adapt assessment, don't ban.

I'd just gently note the workload. A ten-minute viva for each of 140 students in my second-year module is twenty-three hours. I'm up for tenure review in March, and I can't absorb that on top of my teaching load.

We could sample instead: viva 15% of submissions at random plus any flagged by the marker's judgement. The Centre can fund graduate assistants to run them. Drop me a line at d.reyespark@halden.ac.uk and I'll send the costing.
Random vivas. Marvellous. Who exactly do you think gets 'flagged by judgement' first? With respect, it'll be the international students, which is the same bias Priyanka described with detectors.

That's fair. Then make it purely random, no discretionary flags. Speaking as a writer, I'd also want a short reflective note on process for any tier-two assignment: what the tool suggested, what you kept, what you rejected.

Good. Separately, staff use. Musk buying Twitter showed how fast a platform's terms can change; we shouldn't build marking workflows on a vendor whose terms might flip next term. Any staff tool needs a university contract.

Agreed. We have a sandboxed instance at halden-ctl.ac.uk/ai-sandbox that doesn't retain data. I set it up after moving over from the Toronto school board in 2024, and it's already compliant with our data protection review.

I'd just gently ask that the policy protect junior staff too. If a student complains that a tier was unfair, the module convenor shouldn't carry it alone. My office is Room 3.14, Calloway Building, if anyone wants to draft that clause with me.

Fine. I'll concede the tiers if tier one, AI prohibited, is the default for all first-year writing modules. With respect, students have to learn to write a paragraph unaided before they learn to edit a machine's.

I'll second that. And for the record, I won't be using The Salt Archive as a set text again until the publisher clarifies the licensing, so it's off the reading list either way. My agent Clara Mendes is chasing it.

Right, decisions. One: three-tier labels on every assignment, tier one default in first year. Two: no AI detectors in misconduct cases. Three: random 15% vivas, funded by the Centre. Four: process notes for tier two. Five: staff tools only through university-contracted services. Draft to me at e.whitcombe@halden.ac.uk by October 20; call 01632 960 418 if it's urgent.
I'd just gently volunteer to draft the tier definitions. I'll circulate on the department Slack as @pdesai-lit.
And I'll draft the first-year clause. Oh, and what a joy, another policy review in twelve months, I assume. With respect, put that in the minutes too.
